I have been employed as a network engineer for over a decade. I have worked for the military/government, large cloud services providers, and am currently doing consulting work for a ton of different industries. My focus is in core networking (routing/switching), but I also have worked with network security, voice communications, and network services. I am here to answer any of the questions that you have always wanted to ask a nerd.
Is there an issue you encounter when going into a new job, or as a consultant, that consistently makes you cringe?

There're tons of situations that make me cringe. There are a surprising amount of people who are employed to do network engineering that are basically just making it up as they go along. I run into lots of them as a consultant, as most of the people I work for are well aware that they have screwed something up, that's why they're bringing me in.

Here is an example. I recently was looking into the border router setup for a client. they told me they had two internet circuits running BGP going to two routers. Sounds fine, so I ask them how it's all connected. Turns out: both of the circuits, the outside interfaces of the routers, the inside interfaces of the routers, and the outside interfaces of their firewalls are all plugged into the same switch, in the same VLAN. Plus the prefered BGP circuit and the HSRP gateway for their firewalls were not on the same router, so every bit of traffic was being hairpinned on the inside interface of one of the routers.

Edit: I saw that I missed a word.
We're they able to access anything outside the network? Sounds like one giant feedback loop. (Sorry if it's a dumb question, I think I understood most of the comment)

It worked, but was highly sub-optimal. They were running three separate subnets over a single VLAN. They stay mostly separated that way, the big killer is broadcast traffic, whenever an ARP request when out, it hit everything including their ISP's routers.
What has been your favourite employer/client workwise? I. e. where did you have the most interesting things to do and what made it interesting?

So my current work as a consultant goes like this:

I get a project from a customer that has a rough idea of what they want to do. I then meet with the customer and flush out the details of what they want to do and gather an required information. I then write up a 30-100 page technical document that explicitly spells out exactly what is going to be done for the project. That document goes into peer review to cross check everything, then goes back to the customer for approval and possibly revision.

Once they have approved the design, I begin staging and pre-configuring any new equipment. The configured equipment is then shipped out to the customer's site and I oversee the installation of the equipment. I then cut over to the to equipment and make any changes on their existing that are required. Then I write a set of as built documents for the customer's records that highlight everything that was done.

There's a serious fundamental problem with nanomedicine: iterations of the same thing with no conclusive evidence that they improve or will improve treatment outcomes. I work in this space, it's interesting in general and nanoparticles can be a great tool, sometimes. My main contention with this specific report is the use of antiquated therapeutics (paclitaxel) to target cells that would, almost by definition, be resistant. I am still waiting for the day when nanoparticles can be clinically useful and nanotechnology can be improved beyond incremental advancements.

In general, this is not a new type of nanoparticle, we've been making these for decades now. But it would be great to see actual progress in the use of nanomedicine to address challenges like heterogeneity, dissemination or mesenchymal-epithelial transformations.
